news.title: Lithium Market: From End-User Consumption and Active Destocking to the Mismatch in Marginal Procurement [SMM Analysis]1. Core Conclusions The key issue in the current lithium market is not a collapse in end demand, but rather that active destocking across the supply chain has amplified changes in end-user demand, leaving upstream producers facing marginal procurement demand that is significantly weaker than actual consumption. Over the past month, the inventory structure has changed materially: destocking has been concentrated mainly at the downstream level, while inventories held by lithium salt producers and other market participants have increased. This structure suggests that the current inventory drawdown should not simply be interpreted as evidence of strong spot procurement. On the contrary, downstream cathode material producers are meeting production needs by reducing raw material inventories, while remaining cautious on incremental spot purchases. Inventories are gradually shifting from consumption inventories toward producer-held and trading inventories. At the same time, cathode producers do not rely entirely on self-procured lithium salts. Some operate under customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, whereby battery manufacturers, affiliated companies, or designated upstream suppliers provide lithium salts directly to cathode producers for processing. As a result, cathode output and cathode producers’ own lithium salt procurement are not necessarily correlated on a one-to-one basis. When the share of customer-supplied lithium salts rises, cathode production can remain elevated even without a corresponding increase in market-based spot procurement. The market can therefore experience tight supply-demand balances, declining inventories, and weak prices at the same time. The reason is that prices are primarily driven by marginal procurement rather than by end consumption itself. As long as the supply chain remains in an active destocking phase, and part of cathode production continues to be supported by long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts, cathode and battery producers can maintain relatively high production levels while significantly reducing their purchases in the open market. A genuine price inflection point is more likely to emerge when the supply chain shifts from “destocking” to “stable inventories” or even “restocking.” At that point, normal production demand and inventory replenishment demand could be released simultaneously, creating procurement growth that is significantly stronger than the growth in end demand. 2. Total Inventories Are Still Falling, but Inventory Ownership Has Changed From an aggregate perspective, lithium carbonate inventories are still trending lower. However, the structure of this drawdown is notably different from a conventional demand-driven destocking cycle. The most significant feature is that downstream inventories have fallen sharply on a weekly basis, while inventories held by lithium salt producers and other market participants have increased. This indicates that inventory ownership is shifting away from downstream consumers toward lithium salt producers and trading intermediaries. Downstream cathode producers are increasingly operating with lean inventories rather than actively rebuilding raw material stocks during a falling-price environment. Lithium salt producers, meanwhile, have shown some reluctance to sell aggressively at low prices, while trading intermediaries are increasingly performing functions related to price positioning, title transfer, and tactical inventory management. A more accurate description of the current inventory trend is therefore that total inventories are still declining, but inventories are migrating from downstream consumers toward upstream suppliers and intermediate trading channels. This change is important for assessing price elasticity. Downstream inventories primarily serve as production buffer stocks and are relatively rigid, whereas inventories held by traders and lithium salt producers are more price-sensitive. If prices rebound, these latter inventories are more likely to return to the market as potential spot supply, thereby creating upside resistance. 3. Cathode Material Output Has Not Fallen in Parallel, Indicating a Decoupling Between “Consumption” and “Procurement” Cathode material production remains relatively high. According to SMM data, weekly LFP output is approximately 141,600 mt, while ternary cathode material output is around 18,000 mt. Ternary output has declined for nine consecutive weeks, but LFP production remains elevated. Assuming approximately 0.24 mt of lithium carbonate consumption per tonne of LFP, weekly theoretical lithium carbonate consumption associated with LFP production alone would be around 34,000 mt LCE, exceeding the total lithium carbonate inventory reported at cathode producers. This should not, however, be interpreted simply as meaning that downstream inventories are insufficient to support one week of production. First, visible SMM inventory does not capture all lithium salt resources available to cathode producers, which may also include in-transit material, long-term contract deliveries, and raw materials already in the production process. More importantly, customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements are relatively common in the cathode industry. Under such arrangements, part of the lithium salts consumed by cathode producers is not purchased directly by the cathode producer itself, but instead supplied by battery manufacturers, affiliated entities, or designated suppliers. Cathode producers’ visible inventories and self-procured volumes therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to their total lithium salt availability or actual consumption. A more reasonable interpretation is that visible downstream lithium carbonate inventories have been compressed to relatively low levels, but cathode producers can still maintain production through long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and continuous deliveries. This is one of the most important current market features: cathode output has not declined materially, but cathode producers’ own procurement and willingness to purchase in the spot market have clearly weakened. After the pre-holiday restocking cycle ended in October, some cathode producers continued to reduce raw material inventories. Procurement appetite among ternary producers has been particularly weak due to continued production cuts, while LFP producers, despite maintaining high output, have also tended to purchase only on a just-in-time basis, relying more heavily on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and lean inventory management. The market therefore needs to distinguish clearly between “actual lithium salt consumption” and “cathode producers’ own procurement.” Especially when customer-supplied material accounts for a high share of input supply, elevated cathode production does not necessarily translate into stronger open-market buying. 4. Why Can Upstream Orders Weaken Sharply Even if End Demand Does Not? The key relationship is that procurement depends on actual consumption, inventory changes, and the share of customer-supplied material. For a producer relying entirely on self-procurement, procurement can be approximated as: Procurement = Actual Consumption + Change in Inventory For cathode producers that also receive customer-supplied lithium salts, the volume supplied by customers or affiliated parties must be deducted from their own market procurement. Therefore, when cathode producers actively destock while the share of customer-supplied material rises, their market-based procurement can fall well below actual production consumption. For example, assume a cathode producer consumes 100 units of lithium salts per week. If inventories are stable and all material is self-procured, procurement would be approximately 100 units. If the producer actively reduces inventories by 20 units, procurement may fall to 80 units. If a further 20 units are supplied by a customer, the cathode producer’s own open-market procurement may decline to just 60 units. This illustrates that upstream suppliers can experience a sharp contraction in visible buying even if actual production demand is unchanged. This explains why the market can simultaneously observe stable end demand and weak lithium salt buying. The underlying reason is that inventory cycles and supply arrangements jointly amplify changes in end demand. Small changes in end-user demand are transmitted upstream through the supply chain: automakers reduce inventories, battery producers shorten inventory cycles, cathode producers reduce raw material stocks, and long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts further reduce open-market procurement. As a result, lithium salt producers see much weaker effective buying than would be implied by actual end consumption. The weakness in the current lithium market should therefore not simply be attributed to collapsing end demand. A more accurate interpretation is that end consumption and upstream marginal procurement have decoupled, with active destocking and customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements jointly suppressing cathode producers’ demand in the open market. 5. Every Segment of the Supply Chain Is Doing the Same Thing: Reducing Inventory Risk Although the reasons differ across the supply chain, the direction of behavior is broadly the same: reducing inventory exposure. Automakers are relying more heavily on exports to absorb production while controlling domestic channel inventories. Battery producers are shortening inventory cycles and reducing finished cell and raw material stocks. Energy storage project developers, facing mismatches between project construction, grid connection, and delivery schedules, are delaying some product take-up. Cathode producers are reluctant to restock during a falling-price environment and prefer to rely on long-term contracts, customer-supplied lithium salts, and just-in-time procurement. Lithium salt producers are less willing to sell aggressively at prices approaching the cost levels of some higher-cost producers, while trading intermediaries are increasingly shifting from pure distribution toward price positioning and inventory management. Each of these decisions is rational in isolation, but when the entire supply chain reduces inventories simultaneously, the result is a significant reinforcing effect. At the cathode level in particular, active destocking reduces procurement demand, while customer-supplied lithium salts further reduce dependence on the spot market. As a result, the buying seen by upstream producers is materially weaker than actual end consumption. Current prices therefore reflect not only expectations for end demand, but also lower risk appetite and changes in procurement behavior across the broader supply chain. 6. The Mining Segment Is Operating on a Different Timeline: High Imports, High Port Inventories, and Falling Lithium Salt Inventories Can Coexist The upstream mining segment and the lithium salt market currently display very different inventory conditions. China imported approximately 970,100 physical tonnes of spodumene in September, up 7% month on month, including around 136,000 tonnes from Zimbabwe, up 83% month on month. At the same time, domestic port inventories of spodumene remain relatively high, while lithium carbonate inventories continue to decline. These two trends are not contradictory. Between lithium concentrate imports and the eventual production of lithium carbonate, material must pass through several stages, including port arrival, port storage, collection, refinery raw material inventories, feed preparation, conversion, and finished lithium carbonate inventory. This process creates a lag of several weeks to several months. More importantly, when lithium salt prices fall to or below the conversion cost of some externally sourced concentrate producers, or even some lithium residue processors, refinery margins become compressed. Under these conditions, refiners may reduce the pace of port withdrawals, cut spot concentrate purchases, lower operating rates, or defer conversion of certain feedstocks. It is therefore entirely possible for spodumene inventories at ports to remain high while lithium carbonate inventories continue to fall. This means mining supply cannot be assessed using a simple equation of “higher imports = higher lithium salt supply.” The more relevant variables are port inventories, withdrawal rates, refinery margins, and actual operating rates. Among these, refinery margins and withdrawal rates are particularly important because they determine when port-side concentrate inventories are actually converted into lithium salt supply. 7. Why Can Tightness, Destocking, and Weak Prices Exist at the Same Time? The market currently exhibits what appears to be a contradictory combination: relatively tight supply-demand balances, declining inventories, and weak prices. The key reason is that three variables operating across different time horizons are moving simultaneously. First, actual consumption can still exceed incremental supply, which leads to continued inventory drawdowns. Second, downstream participants can actively reduce inventories and increase their reliance on long-term contracts and customer-supplied material, causing self-procurement to remain below actual consumption. Third, the market can price in future supply improvements or slower demand growth in advance, placing pressure on prices. Inventory drawdowns therefore reflect current supply-demand conditions, procurement reflects inventory strategy and supply structure, while prices reflect expected future marginal changes. These three factors do not need to move in lockstep. This also explains why looking only at total market inventories can easily overstate demand strength. The key question is where inventories are declining and who is absorbing them. If inventories are mainly falling at cathode producers while increasing at lithium salt producers and traders, the bullish implication is much weaker than in a scenario where producer inventories are falling and downstream inventories are rising due to active restocking. 8. Three “Gaps” Will Determine When Prices Regain Upside Momentum There are currently three key mismatches across the supply chain that warrant close monitoring. The first is the gap between vehicle production and wholesale volumes on one side, and retail demand on the other. Automakers can absorb production through exports, dealer inventories, and promotions, but as long as retail demand remains insufficient, they will retain an incentive to reduce inventories. The second is the gap between energy storage battery shipments and actual project grid connection. Storage cell shipments do not immediately translate into effective end consumption, as delays can arise from project construction, grid connection, commissioning, and delivery schedules. The third is the gap between cathode material output and market-based lithium salt procurement, which is currently the most directly relevant mismatch for lithium prices. Cathode producers can maintain procurement below theoretical lithium salt consumption by reducing inventories, while customer-supplied lithium salts can further lower their own procurement needs. However, both mechanisms have limits. Inventories cannot be reduced indefinitely, and customer-supplied material merely transfers the identity of the buyer rather than eliminating actual lithium salt consumption. Once raw material inventories approach minimum operating levels and customer-supplied counterparties begin to face their own inventory or procurement constraints, overall supply-chain buying must eventually return to the market. 9. A Genuine Price Reversal Could Be Driven by the Combination of “Production Demand + Restocking Demand” During a destocking phase, market-based procurement remains below actual production demand. When inventories stabilize, procurement gradually converges toward actual consumption. During a restocking phase, procurement can exceed actual production demand. When customer-supplied lithium salts are included, the market must monitor not only a recovery in cathode producers’ own procurement, but also whether the suppliers providing customer-owned material increase their own purchases. Customer-supplied arrangements do not alter final lithium salt consumption; they simply change who is purchasing material in the market. For example, if actual cathode consumption is 100 units, cathode producers may procure only 80 units during a destocking phase. If 20 units are additionally supplied by customers, the cathode producer’s open-market procurement may fall to 60 units. Later, if actual demand rises to 105 units and the supply chain needs to rebuild 20 units of inventory, total supply-chain procurement can increase sharply even if the share of customer-supplied material remains unchanged. This means end demand only needs to improve modestly for procurement growth to be much stronger. The key issue going forward is therefore not whether individual cathode producers increase purchases, but whether lithium salt procurement across the entire supply chain shifts from “distributed customer supply + destocking” toward “active inventory rebuilding.” If several of these inventory gaps begin narrowing around the first quarter of 2027, the lithium salt market could simultaneously receive demand from production recovery and inventory replenishment, thereby amplifying price elasticity. 10. Five Leading Indicators to Monitor The first indicator should be market-based procurement intensity at the cathode level. A simple ratio of “cathode producer procurement / cathode production” can be distorted by changes in the share of customer-supplied lithium salts. A better framework would therefore separate cathode producers’ own procurement, long-term contract deliveries, and customer-supplied lithium salts, and then track self-procurement as a share of actual lithium salt consumption. If cathode production remains stable while both self-procurement and total supply-chain procurement begin to rise, this would be a stronger signal that active destocking is nearing an end. The second indicator is downstream inventory days. Absolute inventory tonnage is less informative than the number of production days covered by those inventories. Inventory coverage should also be assessed alongside long-term contracts, customer-supplied material, and in-transit cargoes to estimate the true minimum operating inventory level. The third indicator is inventory ownership. The key metrics should include the inventory shares held by downstream consumers, lithium salt producers, and traders or other intermediaries. If downstream inventory shares begin to recover while trader inventories decline, this would be more consistent with genuine restocking. The fourth indicator is conversion margins for externally sourced spodumene. Refinery profitability determines when port-side concentrate is likely to be converted into lithium salt supply. If conversion margins remain negative, high port inventories may not translate quickly into higher lithium salt production. The fifth indicator is the combination of basis, warehouse receipts, and spot-market structure. A credible improvement in fundamentals should be accompanied by stronger spot transactions, increased purchasing by cathode producers and customer-supply counterparties, stronger basis, declining warehouse receipts, and stabilization of downstream inventories. If futures prices rise while neither cathode producers nor customer-supply counterparties increase purchases, the rally is more likely to reflect expectations and trading flows rather than a genuine improvement in physical demand. 11. Price Triggers and Validation Framework Three categories of signals should be monitored closely. First, cathode producers’ own procurement and total supply-chain procurement should begin to rise relative to cathode production, which would provide the clearest indication that the inventory cycle is approaching a bottom. Second, the share of inventories held by traders and other intermediaries should decline while downstream inventories stabilize, indicating that inventories are moving back from trading channels into consumption inventories. Third, port-side concentrate pressure should ease, or production cuts among high-cost lithium refiners should materialize, reducing future lithium salt supply pressure. If prices rebound while cathode producers’ own procurement remains weak and customer-supply counterparties also fail to increase market purchases, the underlying weakness is more likely to reflect genuine demand softness rather than a pure inventory-cycle effect. Conversely, if prices remain weak but both cathode producers’ own procurement and customer-supply purchases recover, trader inventories stop rising, and refinery production cuts materialize, the physical market may already be forming a bottom even before prices fully reflect that shift. 12. Conclusion The most important issue in the current lithium market is not simply the size of the supply-demand gap or the fact that inventories are declining, but rather the mismatch between inventory structure, procurement behavior, customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, and end consumption. At present, actual end consumption has not fallen by as much as upstream procurement. Weak prices are increasingly driven by active destocking and changes in the identity of the buyer. Automakers are controlling channel inventories, battery producers are shortening inventory cycles, cathode producers are reducing raw material inventories and lowering their own spot procurement through long-term contracts and customer-supplied lithium salts, some energy storage deliveries are being deferred, lithium salt producers are less willing to sell aggressively at low prices, and trading inventories are increasing. Together, these factors have made upstream marginal buying significantly weaker than actual end consumption. At the same time, inventories are migrating from downstream consumption inventories toward lithium salt producers and trading inventories. As a result, falling total inventories should not automatically be interpreted as stronger demand. From a price-transmission perspective, the key question is not whether end demand suddenly accelerates, but when the supply chain completes its active destocking cycle and lithium salt buyers begin rebuilding inventories. Once cathode inventories approach minimum operating levels, participants shift from “destocking” to “stable inventories” or “restocking,” and customer-supply counterparties also increase their own procurement, normal production demand and inventory replenishment demand could combine to generate upstream order growth well above the pace of end-demand growth. The core market thesis can therefore be summarized as follows: Lithium prices are driven by marginal procurement rather than by end consumption itself. Current weakness reflects the combined impact of the inventory cycle and customer-supplied lithium salt arrangements, while the next price inflection point will depend on when the supply-chain inventory cycle turns positive and when purchasing activity returns to the open market.
